title: A Physiological and Stoichiometric Audit of the Mass Balance Model: Evaluating the Baseline Relative Mass-Outflow-Rate in the Low-Fat vs. Low-Carbohydrate Comparison
content: The Mass Balance Model (MBM) describes changes in body weight using a mass-accounting framework. In its original comparison of isocaloric low-fat and low-carbohydrate diets, the model assigned the same baseline relative mass-outflow rate (R= 0.022) to both conditions. This report conducts an independent physiological and stoichiometric audit of that assumption. The analysis is structured around three distinct levels: mathematical validity, physiological plausibility, and empirical verification. Mathematically, the parameter R is an aggregate of relative mass excretion and an oxygen-uptake correction. Physiologically, carbohydrate and fat oxidation differ substantially in substrate mass and oxygen requirements. However, these differences do not automatically establish that the aggregate parameter R must change, because the individual components of R could theoretically offset one another. A hypothetical sensitivity analysis demonstrates that even a small variation in R (e.g., ±0.002) can produce substantial differences in predicted body-weight trajectories over 56 days, underscoring the importance of the assumption. The analysis does not establish that the common R is incorrect; rather, it identifies a critical assumption whose physiological justification requires direct empirical measurement of diet-specific mass flows.
